text:
The Brief, No. 1

Gulf M&A slowed sharply in the third quarter. Deal value came to about $5 billion, according to Bloomberg data, the lowest level since 2022.

The comparison with last year needs some context. The same quarter of 2025 totalled $69 billion, but $55 billion of that came from a single transaction, the sale of Electronic Arts to an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s PIF. Even allowing for that, activity has clearly slowed, and the fourth quarter has started more slowly still.

The wider MENA region had a stronger first half. EY counted 390 completed transactions worth $46.7 billion across the Middle East and North Africa, many of them negotiated before the regional conflict. The two figures are not directly comparable: one covers the Gulf alone over a single quarter, the other completed deals across the whole region over six months. What they share is the profile of the deals still getting done. Across MENA, transactions above $500 million made up nearly three quarters of total value between March and June, with sovereign funds and government-related entities behind much of it.

For mid-sized companies and family groups considering a sale or a partnership, this may mean a longer search for buyers. We will be watching how the fourth quarter closes.

author: Sagar Bajpai
headline: Managing Partner Antal International | Ex AWS, Google, HCLTech | Leadership Hiring | IT & Non-IT Recruitment | Intelligent Tech, Enterprise
text:
Most “best months to switch” charts are built around the Indian April–March financial year. But many GCCs run on their US or European parent’s calendar year. Their new budgets often open in January, not April.

That changes the timing.

Here’s how I’d think about it:

1. Work backwards from your notice period. With 60–90 days’ notice, an offer in December means a start date in February or March. If you want to join when January budgets open, the time to interview is now.

2. Don’t walk away from your bonus. Check when your current bonus and appraisal pay out. Resigning a month before a payout can quietly cost you lakhs. A good offer should account for it.

3. Specialist roles don’t follow the calendar. When a GCC needs a Cloud Security Architect or an S/4HANA lead, it hires when the need is urgent, not when a chart says so. Senior and niche roles open all year.

4. Quiet months can work in your favour. Fewer candidates in the market means less competition and more attention from hiring managers.

5. Budget resets bring the rush. January and April open new headcount for many companies, and so does every other candidate’s job search. Be ready before then, not during.

So the real question isn’t “which month?” It’s “is my CV ready, and do I know what I’m worth?” If both answers are yes, the month matters much less.

text:
Private equity giants Brookfield and KKR are competing to acquire a controlling stake in Gulf eyewear retailer Eyewa, in a deal valuing the business at around $700 million.

The potential buyout is at an advanced discussion stage, but an agreement depends on the Middle East conflict not escalating further, according to people familiar with the matter.

Founded in 2017, Eyewa started as an online retailer before growing into a regional chain with 250 stores selling contact lenses, prescription glasses and sunglasses across the Gulf.

The retailer raised $100 million in 2024 in a funding round led by US investor General Atlantic. A sale would rank among the region’s first major buyouts since the Iran war began.

Brookfield has raised $2 billion for its Middle East buyout fund, while KKR has deployed around $5 billion in equity across the region since January 2025, reflecting investor interest in Gulf businesses.

However, regional acquisitions have slowed as the conflict weighs on investor confidence and pushes up everyday costs, while households cut spending. Representatives for Brookfield, KKR and General Atlantic declined to comment, and Eyewa did not respond to requests for comment.

text:
Private-sector bank credit in Saudi Arabia hit SAR 3.324 trillion in September 2026. Up 6% year-on-year.

New investment registrations reached 9,018 in Q2 2026. That compares to 2,561 in the same quarter the prior year.

SME financing climbed 16.5% to SAR 490.8 billion. Women now hold 48% of active business registrations. Female labour force participation crossed 33.7%, up from 18% in 2017.

The data points one direction. Capital is flowing into Saudi businesses at scale. The private sector is absorbing it.

Six regions outside the Big Three (Riyadh, Makkah, Eastern Province) posted employment growth above the 7% national rate. Najran led at 45.7%. Hail, Qassim, Northern Borders, Asir, Jazan all above 7%.

Growth is dispersing beyond the main metros. That matters for developers and operators eyeing secondary-city demand over the next cycle.

The SME financing share still sits at 11.7% of total credit. Room to run if Vision 2030 targets hold.

Worth watching if you track Saudi capital deployment.

via Saudi Gazette

Lamprell, L&T Energy Hydrocarbon and Saipem are bidding for Aramco's CRPO 176 offshore package in Saudi Arabia: seven flexible pipelines at the Berri and Marjan fields, worth up to about $400m, and MEED reports Lamprell as the lowest bidder.
Key facts:
• Scope: EPCI of seven flexible pipelines with a combined length of 17 km at the Berri and Marjan offshore fields
• Estimated value: up to about $400m (MEED, 10 September)
• Lamprell emerged as the lowest bidder after evaluation, according to MEED's sources; Aramco is still negotiating with all bidders
• Timeline: tender issued to Aramco's offshore LTA pool in May; bids were due 30 June, extended to 14 July
• The LTA pool has 10 contractors, including McDermott, NMDC Energy, COOEC, Sapura Energy, TechnipFMC/MMHE and Hyundai Heavy Industries
• Same fields, bigger orders: on 23 October NMDC Energy disclosed about $763m for three Aramco packages, eight jackets at Marjan plus production deck modules at Marjan and Zuluf
Why it matters: seven lines and 17 km of flexibles mean orders for flexible pipe, end fittings, bend stiffeners and restrictors, riser protection, buoyancy, subsea connectors and installation-vessel time. Aramco is still negotiating with every bidder, so pipe makers and ancillary suppliers should stay close to all three, not only the low bidder.
